title: What it asks
hook: scholars list its conditions: knowledge, certainty, sincerity, truthfulness, love, acceptance, submission

segments.voice: Yesterday, becoming Muslim: two sentences, said sincerely, the heart left to God. Today, what those sentences ask.

A key with no teeth will slide into a lock and turn nothing. Imam al-Bukhari, at the head of a chapter in his collection, records a saying of an early teacher, Wahb ibn Munabbih. Someone asked him whether la ilaha illallah is the key to Paradise. Yes, he said. But every key has teeth. Bring a key with its teeth, and the door opens for you. Bring one without, and it won't. So what are the teeth? Later scholars tried to name them.

One list some scholars teach is called the conditions of la ilaha illallah. Not extra rules added on, but what it takes for the words to be more than sound. First, knowing. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "So know (O Muhammad) that there is no God save Allah." Know, not just repeat: understand what the no and the yes mean. Second, being sure: certainty, yaqin. The Qur'an describes the true believers as those who believe in Allah and His messenger "and afterward doubt not." Some who teach this list draw a line here: a question passing through the mind isn't the same as doubt that has settled in. Asking is still welcome. Third, sincerity: saying it for God, not for a marriage, a job, or a crowd's approval. The Qur'an says people were commanded to serve Allah "keeping religion pure for Him." Pure there means unmixed, said for one audience. Then the rest of the list: truthfulness, so the tongue and the heart say the same thing; love, for God and for what the words point to; acceptance, taking the whole testimony and not just the comfortable part; and submission, letting it shape what you actually do. Notice what the list is for. Not to sit in judgment over someone else's shahadah; yesterday's story ruled that out, since no one splits open a heart. It's a mirror, held up by people who wanted to check their own key.

Let the list pass slowly through your mind: knowing, certainty, sincerity, truthfulness, love, acceptance, submission, and notice which one catches. Whether you're Muslim or not, you can ask the same of anything you say you stand for: do I know it, am I sure of it, do I mean it? Stay with that one, without grading yourself, and if you pray, ask for help with it.
What it asks. The conditions of the testimony: the teeth on the key, starting with knowing, being sure, and meaning it. Today's word.
Your line: knowing, sure, sincere. Three teeth to start with, out of seven. Up next: oneness, explained.

howItsDone: Some Muslim teachers explain the shahadah through its conditions, using the list as a way for believers to examine their own faith rather than to judge others'.

chat.says: If someone just says la ilaha illallah, is that the whole thing?
options: The words are the key, but it has teeth: knowing, certainty, sincerity, and more.
Yes, as long as you say it in perfect Arabic, with every sound exactly right.
No. Other people have to test the speaker's heart before the words count.
chat.meaning: In Wahb's picture, la ilaha illallah is a key with teeth: knowing it, being sure, meaning it, and the rest of the conditions.

notes: Editor: the conditions list is presented as one list some scholars teach, not the scholars' list; 'much later' and 'scholars who teach this list are careful' softened (teach, myth, trapdoor).
Pickthall 47:19, 49:15 and 98:5 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording (especially 'afterward doubt not' and 'keeping religion pure for Him').
Wahb ibn Munabbih's 'key with teeth' saying is from al-Bukhari's chapter heading (tarjama) in the Book of Funerals, not a numbered hadith; confirm the placement and paraphrase.

The list of conditions follows the index (knowledge, certainty, sincerity, truthfulness, love, acceptance, submission). The script gives no count and calls it 'the list scholars teach'; some scholars add an eighth (rejecting what is worshiped besides God) or arrange it differently. 'Much later' is deliberately vague about when the list was formalized; Keeper may add who.
'Scholars who teach this list are careful here' about passing questions vs settled doubt: a general claim; Keeper to confirm.
The teach ties back to day 1067's Usama story ('no one splits open a heart').
